A guided tour

AI Linc,
end to end.

AI Linc is a learning platform for organisations that train people and then help them get hired. It teaches in the learner’s own language, writes its own courses when the one you need does not exist yet, and reshapes each course around the person taking it. What follows is the product as it runs today, screen by screen, in the order a learner meets it.

See the live demo ↗

Start here

Three things that make it different

Most learning platforms host content you already have, in one language, the same way for everyone. These three are where AI Linc departs from that, and they are the ones worth understanding before anything else.

MODULE 01

Learn in the language you think in

A live tutor that speaks whatever the learner speaks, and keeps the whole lesson in that language, not just the conversation.

AI Tutor

Speak Hindi, Tamil or Spanish, and the whole lesson follows

Most “multilingual” tools translate the chat and leave everything around it in English. Here the tutor mirrors the learner’s language in speech. The material it generates afterwards, including the lesson plan, the practice questions and the recap card, is written in that same language. A learner typing an Indian language in English letters is still understood, which is the case most language detection misses.

  • Mirrors the learnerSpeak or type in your language; the tutor answers in it. Nothing to configure.
  • Not a fixed listThere is no menu of supported languages to pick from. The tutor follows the one the learner actually uses.
  • The whole lesson followsLesson plan, quiz questions and the end-of-session recap are generated in that language too.
  • Romanised script understoodHindi or Tamil written in English letters is recognised, not treated as English.
  • A house language, if you want oneYour organisation can pin a default so the first lesson is in the right language before anyone speaks.
  • Bilingual is a valid answerA programme can run in two languages at once rather than forcing one.
  • Voice or textHold a spoken conversation, or type; a session is 10 or 15 minutes.
  • Grounded in the courseSuggestions come from what the learner is studying right now, not a generic topic list.
  • Confidence-awareNew to this, some idea, or pretty confident: the explanation is pitched to the answer.
MODULE 02

If the course does not exist, make it

A plain-English brief becomes a full course, with weeks, topics, articles, quizzes and coding problems, so your catalogue is never the limit.

Course builder

“8-week Python for absolute beginners, article + quiz per topic”

That sentence is the input. The builder plans the weeks, writes the articles, sets the quizzes and attaches coding problems, and hands you a draft you can edit before anyone sees it. You are not waiting on a content vendor, and you are not limited to what happens to be in the catalogue.

  • Describe it in a sentenceA plain-English brief is the whole input. No course outline required.
  • It writes the courseWeeks, topics, articles, quizzes and coding problems, generated together so they match.
  • Draft first, alwaysNothing reaches a learner until you publish it. Review and edit in between.
  • Build by hand insteadA manual route with no AI, for teams who would rather author it themselves.
  • Or supply an outlineBring a plan as a file and let the builder fill in the material.
  • Verified question bankPractice can be drawn from a checked bank rather than generated on the spot.
  • Edit anythingEvery generated article, quiz and problem stays editable afterwards.
  • Counts you can seeEach course shows its weeks, topics, articles, quizzes and coding problems up front.
MODULE 03

The same course, tuned to each person

A short calibration places the learner, and from then on the course meets them where they are rather than running at one fixed level.

Adaptive personalisation

Calibration sets the level; the course moves with them

Before the real work starts, a short calibration assessment establishes where the learner actually is. After that the course is not one fixed track: quizzes start at the right difficulty, articles open at the right reading tier, and both move as the learner improves. A learner who is finding it easy is not held back, and one who is struggling is not quietly left behind. They can recalibrate at any time.

  • Calibration firstA short placement assessment establishes the starting level before the course adapts.
  • Quizzes start at the right difficultyNot everyone begins at question one of the easy set.
  • Articles open at a reading tierThe same topic, explained at the depth that learner needs.
  • It keeps movingDifficulty follows measured mastery, not a fixed schedule.
  • Recalibrate anytimeIf someone improves quickly, they can reset the baseline rather than grind.
  • Visible to the learnerThe course states the level it has tuned itself to, so it is not a black box.
  • Readiness, not just progressCoverage and performance are scored separately: finishing is not the same as being ready.
  • Feeds the whole systemThe same signal drives the learner’s scorecard and your team’s risk alerts.

1 · The learner

Where a learner begins

The hardest question for someone starting out is not “what is in the catalogue” but “where do I start, and what comes after that”. Roadmaps answer it as a route rather than a list.

Roadmaps

Three ways to choose a route

A roadmap is a path through several courses, laid out as a flow chart. Each box is a real topic the learner can practise and be scored on, so the map is not decoration. It is the syllabus.

  • By roleFrontend, Backend, Full Stack, Data Analyst, Data Engineer, Data Analytics and AI Engineer.
  • By skillJava, SQL, Data Structures and Algorithms, Business Intelligence, Web Performance, C and C++.
  • By employerRoutes shaped for a named company: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini, Cognizant, IBM, LTIMindtree, Tech Mahindra.
  • Core path and optional depthThe flow chart separates what is essential from what is enrichment.
  • Every box is practisableA step is a verified topic with questions behind it, not a heading.
  • Ask for your ownA learner can describe a route in plain English and have one assembled from the verified bank.
  • Numbered stagesThe route is grouped into numbered stages, each holding its own cluster of topics, so progress is countable.
  • Scored at every stepA box is not a heading: it is a topic the learner can practise and be scored on.
  • Assembled, not inventedA requested route is built from the verified question bank rather than generated on the spot.

2 · The learner

Inside a course

A course is not a playlist of videos. It is a board of topics, each holding a mix of reading, watching, answering and writing code, and the learner always knows which single thing to do next.

From course to lesson

Four levels, and never a guess about what is next

The course opens on a board. The board holds topics. A topic breaks into steps. A step is the actual lesson. At every level the learner can see how much is done, how long the rest will take, and what unlocks next.

  • The journey boardEvery topic in the course, in order, with what is finished and what is open.
  • A topic, broken downFor example: 8 steps, made up of 1 article, 1 quiz and 6 coding problems, about 107 minutes.
  • Articles with a check-inReading is confirmed by a question, so progress means understanding rather than scrolling.
  • Video that rewards attentionWatching earns points, with a bonus for not skipping through.
  • Quizzes that adaptDifficulty follows what the learner has actually mastered.
  • Coding in the browserWrite, run against tests, and submit without installing anything.
  • Time estimatesEach topic and step carries how long it should take.
  • Resume exactly where you stoppedOne button returns to the precise step, from anywhere in the product.
  • A stated pass markEach course shows the completion threshold that earns its certificate, so the target is never a guess.

3 · The learner

Practice, and proof it worked

Finishing a course is not evidence. The platform separates what someone has covered from what they can actually do, and turns the second into something they can show an employer.

Assessments

Tests with the state made obvious

  • Five clear statesAvailable, submitted and under review, completed, or expired. Never a question of whether it went through.
  • Known before startingQuestion count, duration, number of sections and the deadline are shown up front.
  • Proctored when it mattersMarked as proctored before the learner begins, with a device check first.
  • Company-shaped papersPractice papers modelled on named employers’ screening tests.
  • Take-home projectsLonger project work alongside timed papers, marked against a rubric.
  • Results that explainA per-attempt breakdown rather than a bare score.

The scorecard and the ladder

One report, and a credential worth showing

The scorecard is the honest version of a learner’s standing: not just what they finished, but how accurate they were, where they are weak, and how they compare with their batch. Certificates sit on a points ladder, so a credential means a measured amount of work rather than attendance.

1,500Learning Foundations
3,000Learning Achievement
5,000Learning Excellence
10,000Skill Readiness
25,000Skill Proficiency
50,000Skill Excellence
100,000Skill Mastery
  • Twelve sectionsActivity, consumption, accuracy trends, skills, weak areas, assessments, interviews, consistency, comparatives, trophies, actions and recommendations.
  • You versus your batchAnd versus the top 10%, so a number has context.
  • Named weak areasSpecific topics needing attention, not a low score with no explanation.
  • Points for real workVideo, article check-ins, quizzes, coding, checkpoints, finals and AI interviews each carry their own weight.
  • Harder work counts moreA difficulty multiplier, so gaming the easy items does not pay.
  • Points decayWeekly windows mean a score reflects current effort, not a burst six months ago.
  • Verifiable credentialEach certificate carries a public verification link.
  • Exports to PDFThe scorecard leaves as a document a learner can send on.
  • Achievements and trophiesMilestones are recorded alongside the numbers, so progress is visible before the next rung is reached.

4 · The learner

Getting hired

For most learners the qualification is the means, not the end. Interview practice, a resume that scores itself, and a jobs board that knows what they are actually eligible for all sit inside the same product.

Interview practice

A live interviewer, on demand

  • Start in secondsPick a topic and difficulty; the questions are generated immediately.
  • Four kindsMixed, technical, behavioural or system design.
  • Three lengths5, 10 or 15 minutes, so practice fits a gap in the day.
  • Spoken, not typedA real-time voice interview with a device check first.
  • Scored and keptAn average and a best score, with every previous attempt retained.
  • Scheduled rounds tooFormal interviews booked ahead and tied to a course.

Resume and jobs

A resume that scores itself, and roles they can actually get

  • Live ATS scoreRecalculates as the learner edits, so the effect of a change is visible immediately.
  • Fixable suggestionsEach one shows the points it would add, with a button to apply it.
  • Six structured sectionsBasic information, experience, education, skills, projects and certifications.
  • Twelve templatesFrom Modern and Minimal to Executive and Technical, exported to PDF in one click.
  • AI tailoringRewrites the resume against a target role.
  • Eight job filtersType, location, experience, skills, employment type, posted, closing and salary.
  • Eligibility statedEach role says whether the learner qualifies yet, and what is missing if not.
  • Apply and track in-appBrowse, applied and saved, without leaving the platform.

5 · The learner

Learning alongside other people

Self-paced does not have to mean alone. Live classes, a forum with its own incentives, and a support queue the learner can actually see the state of.

  • Live classesScheduled sessions with attendance tracked, plus recordings afterwards.
  • A real calendarA month view filtered by batch and course, which syncs to the learner’s own calendar.
  • Attendance that countsSessions attended, attendance rate and live hours, visible to the learner and to you.
  • Five kinds of postQuestion, poll, resource, discussion and the lighter ones that keep a forum alive.
  • Bounties on hard questionsPoints attached to unanswered questions, so they get answered.
  • Verified answersFaculty-marked answers, so the correct one is obvious at a glance.
  • Support with a statusOpen, in progress, resolved and reopened, so the learner is never left guessing.
  • Streaks and standingA leaderboard and streak history that feed the dashboard.

Your team · 01

Running the programme

Everything above is the learner’s view. This is yours: who is enrolled, who is slipping, what is being taught, and whether any of it is working. Your administrators sign in to the same application and switch into an admin view.

The number most platforms bury

How many of them actually showed up

The admin dashboard opens on engagement rather than enrolment, because enrolment flatters and engagement does not. From there you can narrow to one course, change the window, and export what you are looking at.

  • Active against enrolledNot a headcount: how many did something in the period, and the change on the one before.
  • Activities completedVolume of real learning events rather than logins.
  • Median study timePer active day, so one heavy user cannot flatter the average.
  • Tickets waitingSupport left unanswered past its SLA.
  • Six time windows7, 30, 60 or 90 days, 6 months or 12 months.
  • Busiest and quietest dayWhen your learners actually study, which is rarely when you assume.
  • Narrow and exportFilter to a single course, then take the view away as a file.

People

Finding the ones who need you

  • Six risk segmentsAt risk, inactive 30 days, low completion, high performers, never logged in, never active. One click each.
  • Filter and searchBy enrolled course, status, whether they have a saved resume, or by name.
  • One learner, one recordEnrolment, activity, job history and course access on a single page.
  • Cohorts and batchesGroup learners, map them to courses, and run them on their own schedule.
  • Instructors you approveApplications arrive with a CV and are approved or rejected by you.

What you teach, and how you measure it

Courses, papers, credentials and hiring

  • The course builderThe one from the start of this document, in its day-to-day place.
  • Assessment authoringWrite a paper from a brief, or from a blueprint shaped for a named employer.
  • Live monitoringWatch an assessment while it is being taken.
  • Project libraryTake-home projects, auto-graded or marked against a rubric, with a verification queue.
  • Scorecard configurationDefine the skills and badges that learner performance rolls up into.
  • CertificatesTen designs and a seven-rung points ladder you control.
  • Live sessionsZoom and Google Meet both integrated, in a list or a calendar.
  • Interview analyticsTotal interviews, unique students, completion rate and average score, cut four ways.
  • A jobs deskPublish roles to your learners and track applicants, including externally sourced ones.

Your team · 02

Teaching on it

Instructors get a narrower workspace on purpose. They are assigned specific batches and courses, and every page is scoped to that assignment: their students, their gradebook, their classes. One instructor cannot browse another instructor’s learners.

  • A teaching briefingOpens on the single cohort most worth attention this week, and why.
  • Two actions, not a wallOne thing to do this week and one to do today.
  • Their own numbersStudents, cohorts, average progress and how many are at risk.
  • Cohort healthPer-batch progress with a needs-work flag and a full report.
  • Scoped rostersOnly the learners in the batches they teach.
  • GradebookSubmissions for their batches, with the questions and answer key.
  • Classes and attendanceSchedule sessions and record who came.
  • Cohort analyticsProgress distribution across the batches they are responsible for.
  • Marking is not editingBeing given a batch to teach does not grant the right to rewrite its paper; you grant that separately.

Last

Setup and housekeeping

The parts you touch when you start and then mostly leave alone: making the platform look like yours, reaching your learners, and handling the questions they send back.

  • Your own branded instanceYour logo, your colours, your subdomain, your login page wording. Learners see your brand, not ours.
  • Separate certificate brandingA different mark for emails and certificates where you need one.
  • PaymentsConnect your own payment account if you sell courses directly.
  • Email campaignsTracked as jobs, with assessment emails kept separate.
  • Targeted notificationsTo one learner, a course, a batch, or everyone, deep-linked to the right page.
  • Support queueOpen, in progress and resolved, with a named list of who tickets go to.
  • Instructor approvalsThe queue where teaching staff are let in.
  • Only the modules you wantEach part of the platform can be switched on or off for your organisation, so learners are not shown things you do not run.

About this document

How to read it

Every screen here is the live product, photographed as it loaded. Nothing is a mockup, which is worth saying plainly, and so are the caveats below.

  • This is one organisation’s view. The screens come from a demonstration tenant. Your instance carries your branding and only the modules you choose to run, so your sidebar will not match this one exactly.
  • The data is sample data. Learners, cohorts and results are seeded for demonstration. The shapes and the behaviour are real; the numbers illustrate rather than report.
  • Personal details are blurred. Email addresses and phone numbers are masked throughout.
  • Empty is sometimes the honest answer. Where the demonstration organisation has not used a module, the page is shown as it loads rather than dressed up.
  • Captured, not curated. No screen here was staged, retouched or rebuilt for the document.
